title: Plato’s steps to knowledge and Christ
source_text: Καὶ ἄλλην δὲ τοῦ Πλάτωνος λέξιν ἐκτίθεται ὁ Κέλσος οὕτως ἔχουσαν· „ἔτι δὲ μακρότερα περὶ αὐτῶν ἐν νῷ μοι γέγονεν εἰπεῖν· τάχα γὰρ ἂν ὧν πέρι λέγω σαφέστερον ἂν εἴη τι λεχθέντων αὐτῶν· ἔστι γάρ τις λόγος ἀληθὴς, ἐναντίος τῷ τολμήσαντι γράφειν τῶν τοιούτων (καὶ) ὁτιοῦν, πολλάκις μὲν ὑπ᾿ ἐμοῦ καὶ πρότερον λεχθεὶς, ἔοικε δ᾿ οὖν εἶναι καὶ νῦν λεκτέος. ἔστι τῶν ὄντων ἑκάστῳ, δι᾿ ὧν τὴν ἐπιστήμην ἀνάγκη παραγίνεσθαι, τρία, τέταρτον δὲ αὕτη, πέμπτον δὲ αὐτὸ τιθέναι δεῖ, ὅ δὴ γνωστόν τε καὶ ἀληθές ἐστιν· ὧν ἓν μὲν ὄνομα, δεύτερον δὲ λόγος, τὸ δὲ τρίτον εἴδωλον, τὸ τέταρτον δὲ ἐπιστήμη.“ καὶ κατὰ ταῦτα δὲ εἴποιμεν ἂν ὅτι „φωνὴ μὲν βοῶντος ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ“ εἰσῆκται ὁ Ἰωάννης πρὸ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀνάλογον τῷ παρὰ Πλάτωνι ὀνόματι, δεύτερος δὲ μετὰ τὸν Ἰωάννην δεικνύμενος ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ᾧ ἐφαρμόζει τὸ „ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο“, ἀνάλογον ὂν τῷ παρὰ Πλάτωνι λόγῳ. Πλάτων μὲν οὖν τὸ τρίτον φησὶν εἴδωλον. ἡμεῖς δὲ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ εἰδώλου ἐπ᾿ ἄλλου τάττοντες τρανότερον φήσομεν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ γινόμενον μετὰ τὸν λόγον τῶν τραυμάτων τύπον, τοῦτον εἶναι τὸν ἐν ἑκάστῳ Χριστὸν ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ λόγου. εἰ δὲ καὶ ἀνάλογόν ἐστι τῷ τετάρτῳ ὄντι ἐπιστήμη ἡ „ἐν τοῖς“ καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς „τελείοις“ σοφία ὁ Χριστὸς, ἐπιστήσει ὁ δυνάμενος.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus sets out another phrase of Plato thus: 'still longer things about them came into my mind (νοῦς) to say; for perhaps what I speak about would be clearer, these having been said; for there is a true argument (λόγος ἀληθής) opposed (ἐναντίος) to the one who dared (τολμάω) to write anything at all of such things, often said by me before, but it seems to need saying now too. There are, for each of the things that are (τὰ ὄντα), three things through which knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) must come (παραγίνομαι); fourth is it [knowledge]; fifth one must set (τίθημι) the thing itself (αὐτό), which is knowable (γνωστόν) and true (ἀληθές); of which one is name (ὄνομα), second word/definition (λόγος), third image (εἴδωλον), fourth knowledge.' And according to these we might say that 'voice (φωνή) of one crying (βοάω) in the wilderness (ἔρημος)' John was brought in (εἰσάγω) before Jesus, analogous (ἀνάλογον) to Plato's name; second after John, shown (δείκνυμι) by him, Jesus, to whom fits (ἐφαρμόζω) 'the Word became flesh (σάρξ)', being analogous to Plato's logos. Plato says the third is image. We, assigning (τάσσω) the name of image to another thing, will say more clearly (τρανότερον) that the impression/type (τύπος) of the wounds (τραύματα) coming to be in the soul (ψυχή) after the word, this is the Christ in each, from Christ the Word (ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ λόγου). Whether also analogous to the fourth, knowledge, is the wisdom (σοφία) 'among the' [our] 'perfect/mature (τέλειοι)', Christ, the able one will consider (ἐφίστημι).
pass_b_english: Celsus also sets out another passage of Plato, which runs thus: “It has come into my mind to speak still more at length about these matters, for perhaps what I am speaking of would become clearer once this has been said. There is a true argument that stands against anyone who has dared to write anything at all on such subjects; I have often stated it before, yet it seems it must be stated now as well. Each of the things that exist has three things through which knowledge must come; the fourth is knowledge itself; and as a fifth one must set the thing itself, which is knowable and true. Of these, the first is the name, the second the word, the third the image, and the fourth knowledge” (Plato, Seventh Letter 342a–b).

Along the same lines we might say that John, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” (John 1:23; Isaiah 40:3), was brought in before Jesus, corresponding to the name in Plato; and that second, after John, comes Jesus, pointed out by him (John 1:29), to whom the words “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) apply, corresponding to the word in Plato.

Plato calls the third the image. But since we give the name “image” another use, we will say more plainly that the imprint of the wounds that forms in the soul after the word is the Christ in each person, coming from Christ the Word. And whether Christ, the wisdom that is “among the mature” on our side (1 Corinthians 2:6; 1 Corinthians 1:24), also corresponds to the fourth, which is knowledge, let anyone who is able consider.

choices.choice: The quotation is Plato, Seventh Letter 342a–b. The text here reads ἀληθές ἐστιν (‘is true’), translated as given. ἔστι τῶν ὄντων ἑκάστῳ has no connecting particle, so no ‘For’ is supplied. Plato’s λόγος (in the list: name, logos, image, knowledge) means ‘definition’ or ‘account’; it is rendered ‘word’ so that Origen’s comparison with Christ the Word (John 1:14) stays visible. Origen ‘gives the name image (εἴδωλον) another use’ because in Christian usage εἴδωλον means ‘idol’; the pun cannot be kept in English. ‘The imprint of the wounds’ (τῶν τραυμάτων τύπον) is a difficult phrase: it may recall the soul wounded by love (Song of Songs 2:5 LXX, a theme Origen develops elsewhere), the ‘mark of the nails’ (John 20:25), or Christ being formed in the believer (Galatians 4:19); these are possible allusions only and are not cited inline. ἀπὸ Χριστοῦ λόγου may mean ‘from Christ the Word’ or ‘from the word of Christ’; the first is chosen. ‘Pointed out by him’ alludes to John 1:29 (‘Behold the Lamb of God’). ‘The wisdom among the mature’ is 1 Corinthians 2:6; καθ᾿ ἡμᾶς (‘ours’, ‘on our side’) is rendered ‘on our side’; Christ as God’s wisdom is 1 Corinthians 1:24. Origen leaves the fifth term unmatched.
